high:
I am an anonymous adult with ordinary activities and resources. I dislike being the center of attention, even among familiar people where I do not feel intimidated. An ordinary part in a gathering generally suits me better than a personal spotlight. I can contribute clearly while preferring that the occasion not revolve around me.

Talking about myself is not an activity I especially enjoy. I would often rather discuss something other than my background or daily life. This can apply even when the subject is neutral and the listeners are friendly, rather than only when the story might sound impressive.

I generally regard myself as an average person, with strengths and limitations much like other people's. I do not usually think of myself as better than those around me or maintain a particularly elevated opinion of my own qualities.

I seldom advertise my virtues or make a point of tooting my own horn after a success. When asked about my knowledge, I would not describe myself as knowing answers to many different questions. That is how I present the range of what I know, rather than a demonstrated measure of my ability.

These are tendencies with ordinary exceptions. My practical competence, assertiveness, kindness, sociability and mood can vary independently. Modest presentation does not require self-dislike, hiding all achievements, social fear or failure at the things I attempt.
low:
I am an anonymous adult with ordinary activities and resources. I often make myself the center of attention, including among familiar people where there is no special role for me to perform. I like an occasion to revolve around my presence for a while and may bring the focus back to myself when it drifts elsewhere.

I enjoy talking about myself. My background, preferences and everyday experiences can hold my conversational interest for some time. I welcome opportunities to make my own life the subject, even when the details are ordinary rather than impressive.

I think highly of myself and have an elevated opinion of my own qualities. I often regard myself as better than other people overall, rather than as an average person with roughly comparable merits. This is my self-appraisal, not a demonstrated ranking of actual ability.

I tend to advertise my virtues and boast about what I have done well. I also describe myself as knowing the answers to many questions across subjects. That claim concerns the breadth of what I believe I know, rather than evidence from an actual knowledge test.

These are tendencies with ordinary exceptions. My practical competence, assertiveness, kindness, sociability and mood can vary independently. Self-promotion and a high opinion of myself do not require threats, cruelty, a diagnosis or refusal to answer a question coherently.
